articles.text: School board members Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson were appointed to second terms on Piedmont’s Board of Education during the September 23 board meeting. With no other candidates entering the race for the two open seats, the election was canceled, allowing both candidates to retain their seats without a perfunctory vote. Although their names were not on the ballot, current President Medhekar and former president Thomasson sat down with the Post to talk about their renewed terms of service on the school board. Both pointed out that not having to run laborious campaigns has allowed the pair to focus on their biggest task at hand: naming a new superintendent to start January 1, 2027. “It’s been a really great boon. Putting all that energy and devotion into finding the next superintendent, I think and many people agree, is the most important part of the job,” said Medhekar. When Medhekar and Thomasson first won their seats in 2022, the board was immediately tasked with conducting a superintendent search. Now in 2026, they are the vetted and experienced members conducting the search, with returning interim Superintendent Donald Evans leading the hunt. Board members Max Roman, Susy Struble and Michael Malione have two years under their belts too, making the whole board confident they can find a great new superintendent. The board has received more than 300 surveys regarding the most desirable qualities in a Piedmont superintendent. articles.text: Three years after powerful winter storms toppled trees, knocked out power and triggered landslides in Piedmont, city officials say they are better prepared for another potentially severe winter. At the October 19 City Council meeting, city officials outlined the measures they have taken to protect the city ahead of an El Niño that forecasters warn could be among the strongest on record. Earlier, California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency in anticipation of severe weather. “In the New Year’s 2023 storm series … we had significant impacts, including trees, localized flooding, and some landslides. Facing these risks really informs how we prepare,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, adopted in March, identifies areas vulnerable to natural disasters and outlines measures to reduce those risks. City officials say they have begun addressing some of those vulnerabilities through infrastructure improvements and emergency preparations. The city realized that unreliable communication between departments was a problem as the call volume increased. Brannigan said the department received 26 calls in one 24-hour period during the 2023 storm, compared with a typical three to five. They’ve fixed this by upgrading the household-level radios used by Public Works, which were inadequate for emergency communications. Police, fire, and Public Works personnel are also conducting joint emergency response drills to work on communication during high traffic. Piedmont upgraded its backup power systems after the power outages during the 2023 storms. Now, with the new Dispatch Center, they have a more substantial generator and isolated power supply that can power the entire Veterans Building and ensure uninterrupted 911 services. They’ve set up a system where staff regularly check fuel levels in the generators at the Corporation Yard to ensure they are ready for extended power outages. Public Works Director Bonnie Tam cited the bioswale on Grand and Fairview avenues and upgraded storm drains at eight locations as examples of the city’s infrastructure investments. Each year, the city cleans out 480 catch basins, prunes 1,000 trees, and conducts additional street sweeping during the fall season as preventative maintenance. “This work we continue throughout the year is to make sure we provide the foundation for seasonal preparations. To prepare for the storm this season, we will really focus on known problem locations,” said Tam. To prepare for potential heavy rains, the city has ordered 1,100 feet of wattles stuffed with compost and straw. The wattles protect storm drains from debris that would block water flow and potentially cause flooding. The city has also secured several contractors that will be able to work during emergencies. The Public Works team is actively monitoring 46 potential trouble areas like creeks, catch basins, sewer mains, and sewer mains. “When significant storms are predicted, our staff will be able to stay at the Corporation Yard overnight to make sure we can respond to emergencies. We have enough personnel, expertise and equipment at the yard that we can deploy,” said Tam. Support Services Commander Jodi Cornell outlined how Piedmont’s Police Department will prepare for the storm. “In anticipation of significant storm activity, Chief Shavies will increase staffing levels as operational conditions warrant,” Cornell said. “Additional personnel will help manage increased coverage throughout the city, responding to calls for service, weather-related emergencies, and maintaining public safety coverage.” The city recommends that residents prepare their homes for the winter storms by clearing drains and gutters, checking indoor flood protections, and keeping flashlights or lanterns available for power outages. During major storms, the city’s website will post continual updates on conditions and impacts until the storm subsides The Public Works Department is giving out 10 free sandbags per household at the city’s Corporation Yard (898 Red Rock Road) from 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Carriage House Salon is hosting a lecture titled “A Journey through Long Lost Oakland” on Sunday, November 8, from 3 to 5 p.m. Lecturer Liam O’Donoghue will explore a historical map he developed and the many transformations Oakland has experienced. From stunning architecture to bygone infrastructure and even extinct plants and animals. The event will be held at the Pardee Home Museum at 672 11th Street, Oakland, entering through the gate on Castro Street. O’Donoghue hosts and produces the East Bay Yesterday podcast and KPFA radio program. His journalism has appeared in Mother Jones, Salon, Snap Judgment, and 99 Percent Invisible. O’Donoghue has lectured on local history at libraries, schools, and bookstores throughout the Bay Area, as well as at institutions such as the California Historical Society, Oakland Museum of California, Berkeley City Club, and Commonwealth Club. His show has been called The Best Podcast about the East Bay by the East Bay Express, and he has been honored by Oakland Heritage with a “Partners in Preservation Award.” Following the lecture, guests will enjoy a Champagne reception with sweets and savories. Call Richelle Lieberman at 510- 381-1973 for reservations. Tickets are $25 per person. All proceeds go directly to the museum.

articles.text: Community organizers and Piedmont residents Dick Carter and Lisa Gardner are starting a singing group for people of all ages. Piedmont Singin’ 4 Fun will offer adults an opportunity to sing together for fun and companionship, regardless of musical ability, and address a growing need for socializing amid concerns about loneliness, particularly among older adults. As Carter and Gardner began work on the Adult Recreation Expo in November, they noticed a gap among community organizations for music and singing. “There really weren’t any activities or groups other than maybe religious groups that offered the opportunity for regular people to come and sing,” said Carter. So he decided to start his own. Groups like this one, Walking on Wednesdays and Piedmont Seniors, offer opportunities for socializing and building friendships. Research indicates that meaningful choice of activity, training, and ongoing support were associated with socioemotional benefits, and the researchers concluded that meaningful engagement can improve older adults’ psychological well-being. Carter’s own experience suggests that older residents are looking for more ways to connect. “As they transition out of the workforce and change lifestyles, many older adults are looking for activities that foster social connectivity. It’s in the media too. The ‘loneliness epidemic’ is an issue, and there is an understanding of how critical peer relationships are to healthy aging,” said Carter. Older adults continue to participate because of the enjoyment of whatever the activity is and, just as importantly, the community they experience in the groups. Events like the Adult Recreation Expo bring together community organizations and invite residents, encouraging them to interact with these groups and find an activity they enjoy. Each year the expo draws about 150 attendees and representatives from about 50 community organizations. The group’s first meeting will take place Tuesday, November 10, at 801 Magnolia Avenue from 11 a.m. to noon. The group will start with a collection of about 10 easyto-sing songs, adding more to the repertoire over time. Expect a variety of upbeat, positive music, with song sheets provided so everyone can follow along. Carter and Gardner will host a booth for their new singing group at the expo on November 15. Those interested in joining the group can attend the expo and meet the organizers there or email Carter directly at camktgrp@comcast.net.

articles.text: Looking for a pair of deeply bonded beauties? Piedmont Singin’ 4 Fun will offer adults an opportunity to sing together for fun and companionship, regardless of musical ability, and address a growing need for socializing amid concerns about loneliness, particularly among older adults. articles.text: Teaching & Learning Officer, Exploratorium You’ve probably heard the predictions: a powerful El Niño is developing, potentially bringing a wetter, stormier winter to California. But what exactly is El Niño? And what happens when it collides with some of the highest tides of the year? This November, families across the Bay Area have an opportunity to explore these questions together. First, a little science. Every few years, a natural climate cycle called El Niño occurs when a specific region of the eastern tropical Pacific becomes unusually warm (at least 0.5°C above average for several consecutive months, to be exact). The warmer water changes where storms form over the tropics, and this ripples out to weather around the globe, often increasing the likelihood of rain in California. El Niño also temporarily raises sea levels along our coasts, sometimes by several inches to a foot, due to warmer water taking up more volume and stronger storms pushing water against the shore. Now add King Tides to the mix. King Tides are the highest predicted tides of the year, occurring when the gravitational forces of the sun and moon combine to produce especially dramatic tidal changes. They’re natural and predictable, but their effects can be amplified when ocean levels are already elevated due to El Niño, or storms roll through. Water can reach farther inland, sometimes flooding low-lying areas in Alameda, Berkeley, Marin County, and along San Francisco’s Embarcadero. One of my family’s first lessons in King Tides came from Exploratorium science educator Lori Lambertson, who has spent years helping teachers and the King Tides occur when the gravitational forces of the sun and moon combine to produce especially dramatic tidal changes. public understand this phenomenon. My daughters still remember pulling on their rain boots and walking the piers near the museum with Lori as unusually high water splashed up and over the railings! Our next round of King Tides will arrive in the Bay Area November 24–26. It’s a fascinating opportunity to observe and explore the forces shaping our shoreline, while being mindful of changing waterfront conditions. Start by becoming tide detectives. Look up local tide predictions together. Ask younger kids to share what they notice about the tide graph shapes for a day and older kids why those peaks and valleys make sense. Together, guess how high the water might rise or when you might want to wear shoes you don’t mind getting wet! As curiosity grows, you might explore how the moon’s position influences tides or investigate why some neighborhoods are more vulnerable to flooding than others. If conditions permit, take a field trip to a waterway during a peak tide period and observe from a safe, elevated viewpoint. What looks different? Which areas are underwater? What might happen if the water rose a little bit more? There’s a bigger lesson here, too. As global sea levels rise, today’s King Tides offer a glimpse of what ordinary high tides could look like in the future. How might our communities need to adapt? What could we do differently? Another place to get curious is taking shape at the Exploratorium. The Waterfront Field Station, a free outdoor learning space currently under construction along the Embarcadero, will soon invite visitors to explore rising tides, shifting shorelines, and the science behind our changing Bay. This November, take a closer look at the Bay. Notice what’s changing, ask questions, and see what you can discover together. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class is thrilled to present Peter Pan and Wendy by Lauren Gunderson. This charming, empowering reimagination of J.M. Barrie’s classic Peter Pan follows Wendy Darling, played by junior Lucy Shoop, after just finding out her parents are sending her to finishing school. Wendy, wishing to win a Nobel Prize, rejects this demand. After stumbling on Peter Pan, played by junior Miles Simon, Wendy takes her younger brothers, John and Michael (senior Yiyou Fang and junior Eli Mittan), on an adventurous journey to Neverland. There, the family and the Lost Boys battle with the bloodthirsty Captain Hook (junior Zayd Mahmood) and his pirates for control and glory. Sophia Puckett, who plays the pirate Smee, says “the play teaches the audience to enhance their imagination and to not give up on their aspirations. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School 7/8 orchestra, led by teacher Shauna Revelli, performed Halloween ballads in front of the Buzz Redford Gym as students arrived to campus on Friday, October 30. Piedmont Middle School celebrated Halloween on Friday, October 30 with costumed fun and a lunchtime carnival that got nearly the entire faculty and much of the student body participating in the masquerade. Halloween on campus kicked off with moody music in the morning and concluded with a spirited costume contest. The seventh- and eighthgrade orchestra performed before school’s first bell to help set off a nice “spooky” vibe for the kickoff to the Halloween weekend. The 7/8 Orchestra, directed by Shauna Revelli, played The Addams Family, The Ghost of John, Danse Macabre, In the Hall of the Mountain King and Spooky Night. The music out on the patio filled the steps of students with Halloween pep as they headed to their first period classes and a day of make-believe. The lunchtime activities at PMS included a Halloween Carnival, which was arranged by the Associated Student Body (ASB) class. Science teacher Laurel Marinho is the teacher of the ASB class and guided the production of the holiday event. “Dressed as the aliens from Toy Story, ASB students ran carnival games like ball toss and plinko, where all students played to win some candy. They also hosted a costume contest with prizes for scariest, most original, funniest, and ‘most aura.’ From Men in Black to Homer Simpson, the variety and creativity of student costumes did not disappoint!” said Marinho. Teachers and staff across the district got in on the Toy Story theme, and some middle school departments, like Physical Education and Science expertly coordinated their costumes too. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont goes into Friday’s season-finale against Alameda with a chance to gain an NCS post-season berth. Piedmont High’s football team got back in the win column on Friday, October 30 at Pinole Valley, winning 31-16 at the Spartans’ home field. The result improves the Highlanders’ record to 3-6 overall with one game left in their regular season. The Highlanders led 24-0 through the third quarter, including a 17-0 lead at halftime after forcing a pair of turnovers. “Big contributions from special teams. The defense tackled really well and forced turnovers. That’s a good win for the program and the kids, we’ve been in some tough games and it really showed our mettle. To finish was good, we had our opportunities in our recent games. We talk all the time about having a one game and missing one play here and there, that’s been our bugaboo all year,” coach Jordan Seiden said. articles.text: Highlanders beat San Leandro, Clayton Valley 3-0 Staff Photos Piedmont celebrates their NCS Quarterfinals win over Clayton Valley Charter. As a result, the Highlanders qualified for their first NCS Semifinals appearance since 2008. Piedmont High’s 2026 girls’ volleyball team has solidified itself among its best of all time. As the No. 3 seed in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs, the squad opened with a 3-0 win over No. 14 San Leandro on Tuesday, October 27 at the Pirate’’ gym, and followed up with a 3-0 win over No. 11 Clayton Valley Charter at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, October 31 in the quarterfinals. They are scheduled to face No. 2 Justin-Siena in Napa today, November 4, in the NCS Semifinals. It marks the first time the school has reached the round since 2008. Their first-round win was the program’s first NCS victory since 2015. “I was not even born yet. It means the world to me for us to make it this far. I’m really proud on top of all the academics we do; we barely sleep and we’re always grinding,” junior Allyson Huynh said. “It’s really exciting. As a junior, it gives me a lot of hope for next year because we have such a well-developed team of underclassmen,” said junior Maika Ting. Moreover, their 17-13 record is the school’s most wins in a season since they went 19-11 in 2013. “Today was one of the best games we ever played. At the start of the season, we were a little slow to make changes. But this game, we studied the game plan, made changes fast, and trusted each other,” Huynh said. Making a big impact against Clayton Valley was Izara Dando, leading the team with 10 kills. She filled into the middle role late in the regular season following an injury to Charlotte Bailey, and has proven productive in the middle, outside hitter, and opposite hitter positions. “It comes from what we do in practice. It means a lot to get more playing time, so I want to take advantage of every moment I can. I really like the middle role because you can take control and it’s a lot of fun. We’re playing really well, we’ve really come together as a team in terms of our communication and togetherness on the court,” Dando said. 3-0 over Clayton Valley Piedmont swept the Eagles by scores of 25-14, 25-10, 26-24. Despite Piedmont’s 11-point win in the first set, there were two lead changes before Piedmont took control at 13-12. From there, PHS closed with 12 of the final 14 points in the set, including the last eight of nine. Piedmont owned the second set from the get-go. The Highlanders held a narrow 9-7 lead early on, and then scored the following eight of nine points with kills by Dando, Ting, and Nora Trombi, along with two aces by Mia Bechtel and one by Hazel Schaeffer. At 17-9, PHS scored the final eight of nine as well with kills by Dando, Lucia Dorsey, Charlotte Bailey, and two by Maika Ting sends a spike against Clayton Valley.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team finished third in the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament with a pair of wins and a semifinals loss at the San Leandro High pool. As the No. 3 seed, the boys opened with a 13-6 win over No. 5 Castro Valley on Tuesday, October 27, lost in a heated 9-8 semifinals match to No. 2 Berkeley two days later, and finished with an 11-8 win over No. 4 Bishop O’Dowd in the third-place final on Saturday, October 21. Their semifinals loss marked the third time Piedmont fell to the Yellowjackets this season by just one goal after losing 10-9 on September 4 and 13-12 on September 29. Piedmont’s 11-8 victory over Bishop O’Dowd was the fourth time the two sides played each other this season, with the Highlanders winning all four matches. “Berkeley is a very good team. They executed, but I thought we played really well. We had a couple of lapses on guarding their offensive players, and exclusions kind of put us in the hole… [With O’Dowd] it’s hard to beat a team four times, but it’s also hard to beat a team three times like Berkeley just did. At this point of the season, our focus is on NCS, so we take each game and find ways to improve,” coach Rik Krumins said. The result could’ve easily gone the other way against Berkeley if one or two plays went another way. They committed a costly turnover near their own net near the end of the second quarter, which led to a Berkeley goal. Piedmont also failed to convert a breakaway opportunity in the third. “You don’t expect those moments. You think as a coaching staff that we had everything covered, but we didn’t. It’s a little immaturity and a mental lapse, but we’ll grow from that,” Krumins said. The Highlanders now earned the No. 16 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section bracket. They are set to face No. 1 Northgate at Las Lomas in Walnut Creek tomorrow, November 5. 13-6 over Castro Valley PHS scored the opening three goals to lead 3-0 with 2:37 left in the first quarter with scores by Henry Van Den Bos, Rylan Patty, and Oliver Hurwitz. CV cut the lead to 3-2 by the 1:20 mark, but Patty scored one minute later to make it 4-2. Piedmont scored three unanswered goals in the second quarter to extend their lead to 7-2 with 2:40 left, including two goals by Patty and one by Henry Stein. The Trojans scored one before halftime with three seconds left. In the third, Patty scored 36 seconds in, while Walker Wilson made it 9-3 at the 5:50 mark. CV scored nearly 40 seconds later, but it was their only goal in the quarter. Stein made it 10-4 with 4:57 to go, followed by Patty making it 11-4 with 29 second left. After an initial goal by CV in the fourth quarter at 5:13, PHS added its final two goals by Stein at the 4:55 and 3:35 marks. The Trojans got its final goal with 3:06 remaining. Final scorers: Patty had six goals, Stein had four, while Hurwitz, Wilson, and Van Den Bos had individual goals. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country concluded its regular season at a Western Alameda County Conference meet on Wednesday, October 28 at Oyster Bay Regional Park in San Leandro. The boys’ squad finished fifth of nine teams, while the girls’ varsity team was unable to score with just four of five required runners available. The Highlanders now prepare for the 2026 Western Alameda County Conference Championship race at Hayward High on Saturday, November 6. “With the league championships approaching, this was another opportunity for our runners to test themselves against familiar competition and see how their fitness has progressed throughout the season. We’re entering the final stretch of the season, and it’s encouraging to see so many runners continuing to improve after nearly three months of training and racing,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Senior Alex Schleuning led the way, finishing 13th of 76 runners with a time of 17:06.3 on the three-mile course. “Alex improved by 55 seconds over his performance on this course last year, setting a new course personal record. This was an excellent performance as we approach the championship portion of our season,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Schleuning was sophomore Dylan Wallway, placing 30th in 17:53.5. Rounding out their best five times was sophomore Blake Riif in 33rd in 18:02.6, junior Luca LaForte right behind Wallway in 34th in 18:05.6, while freshman Cormac Ross placed 38th in 18:07.7. “Dylan Wallway was our second finisher, followed closely by Blake Riiff, Luca LaForte, and Cormac Ross. Blake’s performance was particularly encouraging. He finished as our third runner and earned a season-best performance relative to the competition, continuing to establish himself as a strong contributor to our varsity squad. Luca also had an excellent race, improving his previous Oyster Bay performance by 48 seconds and setting a new course PR,” Zirkelbach said. The girls team has been hampered by injuries throughout the year and have been without senior Leighton Mand and sophomore Kelsey Coleman the entire 2026 campaign. They’ve also missed out on senior Amalia Gray for all but one race this season. Junior runner Viviane Oesterer has remained a bright spot for the squad. She placed fifth overall out of 63 athletes, clocking a time of 19:43. “Viviane Oesterer continues to impress, she delivered another excellent race. Her time represents an improvement of one minute, 45 seconds over her performance on this course last year, an impressive 8.2 percent improvement. She also established a new course personal record, improving her previous best of 20:07 by 24 seconds. Her continued development has been one of the highlights of our season,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Oesterer was senior Cora Brozowski-Schrader, finishing 22nd in 21:00.8. Behind her was sophomore Madeleine Ewen in 38th in 22:14.1, and senior Annie Thornton in 41st in 22:49. “Cora improved by 29 seconds over her previous performance on this course. Cora continues to demonstrate the strength and experience that have made her an important contributor to our varsity team. Madeleine Ewen recorded a season-best performance relative to her competition and a new three-mile distance personal record. Annie Thornton delivered one of the day’s biggest improvements, making an impressive one minute, 20 seconds off her previous Oyster Bay performance,” Zirkelbach said. articles.text: In their season finale on Saturday, October 24, Oakland Roots fell 3-2 on the road to Sacramento Republic FC after holding a 2-1 lead as the game entered its final 10 minutes. Roots were playing for a final playoff spot, and for a moment, it looked like they were headed to the postseason. Oakland needed to win on Saturday at Sacramento and have eighth-place Phoenix Rising lose or tie in order to catapult past Phoenix for the eighth spot for a final playoff seed. On Saturday night, Lexington trailed 3-1 before tying Phoenix 3-3 as Roots’ match raged on. At that point, Roots controlled their destiny, and just needed to hold on. But, like an epic body blow, Sacramento equalized in the 81st minute before landing the haymaker finish in the 90th minute to put Oakland behind. The match went from supreme hope for Roots’ fans to supreme dread. Oakland’s season is officially over, finishing 10th place in the West. Sacramento opened the scoring in just the second minute when a short-played corner kick led to a shot from the right side of the box by Alfredo Midence. Roots leveled in the 45th minute when a free kick was given in the attacking third. Jesus De Vicente sent a pass into the penalty area before the ball deflected to Danny Trejo to make it 1-1. Just five minutes later in firsthalf stoppage time, Roots took the lead when De Vicente made a run up the left side before putting an inch-perfect cross to Peter Wilson behind the backline. Around the 60th minute in Roots’ match, Lexington tied Phoenix 3-3 to put Oakland’s traveling fans into a frenzy. But Sacramento won the free kick that led to its equalizer. In the 81st minute, a pass from Memo Rodriguez by way of a free kick led to a header by Lee Desmond to knot it up at 2-2. Then in the 90th minute, Republic put the dagger into the game. With Oakland committing numbers forward on a corner, Sacramento burst on a counterattack the other direction, leading to Kyle Edwards ending Roots’ playoff dreams. Oakland ends their season Oakland Roots suffered a dramatic 3-2 loss at Sacramento Republic to end its 2026 season. Staff Photos

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera Guild will host its 13th annual “An Evening on the Stage” gala dinner November 17 at the War Memorial Opera House, honoring General Director Matthew Shilvock with the organization’s Crescendo Award. The award recognizes individuals for their support of the guild and San Francisco Opera. The evening’s musical program will feature mezzo-soprano Daniela Mack performing selections from her debut solo album, Sur, featuring songs by Astor Piazzolla arranged by Juan Pablo Jofre. Jofre will accompany Mack on bandoneón, along with pianist Ronny Michael Greenberg and members of the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. The San Francisco Opera Guild Opera Scouts will also perform. French composer Jules Massenet’s version of Manon has a French outlook. In the version by Puccini (based on the exact same story by novelist Abbé Prévost), the outlook is completely Italian. Manon is the life story of the beautiful courtesan Manon, including her many adventures and her tragic death on the shores of Louisiana. We get to experience beautiful life, intrigues, murder and assassination. Sounds like modern life, doesn’t it? To this vivid story, the composers have added music. That’s why opera was and continues to be so popular. And now to the San Francisco opera production of Manon by Massenet. Fortunately, the strike by the San Francisco opera members has been settled. They took their place in the pit, and then the opera began. The San Francisco Opera, like the Metropolitan Opera, has some of the finest musicians in the country. They deserve to have a music director who has the same qualifications. I am not convinced of this. As for the production, the costuming was elegantly beautiful and the singers possess fine voices. In the title role of Manon was Amina Edris, and her lover, des Grieux, was played by Pene Pati. Both singers possess fine voices, but Edris is a much better actress, putting on a convincing performance. In general, the acting was perfunctory. When the two singers were singing love duets, they were placed at opposite ends of the stage. There was no embrace. Thirty to forty feet separated the two lovers. Staging like this is absolute nonsense. Diction is another ongoing problem. The dialogue and singing are in French. However, it was impossible to know what language they were singing. The dialogue was marginally better… but not by much. As for the singing, it was unintelligible. I remember seeing Puccini’s version of this opera many years ago. In his version, the story was more vivid and also more brutal. Nonetheless, the overall performance of San Francisco Opera was enjoyable. As the French expression goes… “Vive la différence.” French composer Jules Massenet (left) and Italian composer Giacomo Puccini (right) used the same story for their operas. Both wrote monumental operas on Manon.

articles.text: Tickets on sale now The San Francisco Ballet’s 2026-27 season begins on December 4 with the holiday favorite Nutcracker, set in San Francisco and honoring the company’s legacy as the first American company to present a full-length production of the ballet. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet presents the production every year and features a cast of more than 150 dancers within the company to tell the classic holiday story. Former artistic director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production was inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by a live orchestra that performs Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. A diverse array of instruments is played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani. Michael Yeargan is scenic designer, Martin Pakledinaz designed the costumes and James F. Ingalls designed stage lighting for Nutcracker. A sensory-friendly performance will be held at 11 a.m. on December 27. The matinee production features special accommodations for those who experience sensory processing disorders, autism, post-traumatic stress disorder, and all neurodiverse audiences. It takes place in a relaxed and “shush-free” setting and is appropriate for all ages, and designated quiet areas will be available for guests. Showtimes vary. Visit https:// www.sfballet.org/2026-2027-season/ to purchase tickets. Past production of San Francisco’s Nutcracker

articles.text: An exhibition at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco explores how photographers helped shape the image of Paris through photographs documenting the city’s architecture, cultural heritage and transformation into a modern metropolis. Eternal Paris: Photographing the City of Light is on view now, featuring nearly 50 photographs from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts, many of which have never been exhibited publicly. The exhibition traces the work of photographers in the 19th and early 20th centuries who documented Paris’ historic landmarks, preserved its architectural heritage and captured the changes that reshaped the city. Their images helped establish Paris as an international center of art and culture. Among the works are early photographs of the city’s celebrated monuments, images of the ruins left by the Paris Commune of 1871 and photographs documenting Paris as it stood on the threshold of modernity. The exhibition also features works by photographers including Édouard-Denis Baldus, Eugène Atget and Brassaï. Atget is known for his extensive photographic documentation of Paris, recording its streets, buildings and neighborhoods during a period of significant urban change. Together, the photographs show how the medium helped preserve the city’s past while documenting its evolution. Eternal Paris: Photographing the City of Light is on view at the Legion of Honor, 100 34th Ave. in San Francisco, through February 28, 2027. For information, visit famsf. org/exhibitions/eter nal-paris-photographing-city-light. Legion of Honor

articles.text: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes film lives up to the hype Calling You Can See Everything a documentary doesn’t feel quite right. Documentaries are supposed to lay out the facts and seek the truth, which is why, for most of them, you could skip the ticket and just read the Wikipedia article. Not this one. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film about Elizabeth Holmes, the Stanford dropout whose Palo Alto startup Theranos became Silicon Valley’s most notorious fraud, isn’t interested in rehashing facts already covered in the book Bad Blood and Hulu’s The Dropout. Instead, it’s a character study in manipulation. After nearly three hours, I’m not convinced there was ever any truth to be found, but that’s part of the appeal. Few movies this year have arrived with this much buzz, and almost none arrived so quietly. Shot in secret over three years, the film debuted unannounced at the Telluride Film Festival in September, along with a shadow-dropped trailer: a single, mostly silent scene of Holmes staring down a visibly uncomfortable Fielder. The Oscar talk started almost immediately, and A24 is now campaigning it for Best Picture; even a nomination would be a first for a documentary. The hype has paid off at the box office, too, with the second-biggest opening ever for a non-music doc. The premise: 34 days before reporting to federal prison, Holmes invited Fielder and a small crew into her rented San Diego beach home to document her final weeks of freedom. It’s an odd choice: Fielder, the deadpan comedian behind Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, is a master manipulator of his subjects and audience, the last filmmaker you’d expect Holmes to trust. But he may have met his match in a woman who once convinced some of the most powerful people in America that her blood-testing machines could do the impossible. Rounding out the trio is her partner, Billy Evans, whose murky intentions make him a potential manipulator, too. This is no fly-on-the-wall doc, either. Fielder ends up under the same microscope as his subjects, and the real question becomes less “What did Elizabeth Holmes do?” and more “Who is manipulating whom?” At times, he seems to steer you toward casting Evans as the villain and Holmes as his victim, but nothing in this film is quite what it seems, including the relationship at its center. Without giving anything away, it takes a sharp Fielder-esque turn partway through and becomes something else entirely. The less you know going in, the better. What I can say is that it looks nothing like a typical documentary. Fielder and Oppenheim shoot it with a cold, almost David Fincher-like precision: muted colors, deliberate framing, and an unsettling stillness that makes the Holmes household feel more like a set from Gone Girl than a home movie. Extreme, tension-filled close-ups leave you staring into their faces for uncomfortably long stretches, searching for any flicker that might reveal whether they’re being truthful. And forget the nicely lit interview rooms of most documentaries; here, you’re in their bedrooms, their living room, and even their shower. It’s also funny. Often called his generation’s Andy Kaufman, Fielder constantly blurs perforNathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything is in theaters now. mance and reality, and many of the laughs here come from his general creepiness as he lurks in the shadows, like a houseguest who doesn’t respect personal space. One of the funniest moments comes when he sits Holmes down to watch Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First?,” a sketch about two people endlessly talking past each other, which feels more than a little on the nose in how the scene plays out. At 174 minutes, it’s a long sit, but I never once checked my watch. It’s one of the most original, unsettling, and entertaining films of the year, documentary or otherwise. Skip the Wikipedia article on this one. You have to see it for yourself. Just don’t expect to walk out knowing who to believe. You Can See Everything is rated R (not for kids) and runs 2 hours, 54 minutes. Now playing at Landmark’s Piedmont Theatre, 4186 Piedmont Ave., Oakland.

articles.text: With stress and anxiety increasingly affecting our world, more children than ever are receiving mental health services. Interacting with a dog may help establish trust and make children more comfortable engaging with their therapist. Simple activities such as petting, brushing, or quietly sitting beside a dog can offer a calming sensory experience. articles.text: One of the joys of movies is watching them with friends and discussing them afterward. The 2nd Thursday at the Movies group, previously known as the Flix Fest, meets on the second Thursday of each month, offering movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussions. November’s featured movie is 1992’s A Few Good Men, a gripping courtroom drama. Rob Reiner as director and producer skillfully explores the moral and legal boundaries of the Marine Corps code of conduct. The story unfolds when following orders leads to the tragic death of Private William Santiago at the Marine Corps base in Guantanamo Bay during the post-Cold War period. Colonel Nathan R. Jessup (Jack Nicholson) orders Lt. Jonathan Kendrick (Kiefer Sutherland) to execute the Code Red instead of granting Santiago a transfer back to the States. Kendrick chooses Lance Corporal Dawson and Private Downey to perform the hazing in the dead of night, ensuring no witnesses. Santiago’s unanticipated death prompts Col. Jessup to initiate a cover-up. Simultaneously, Dawson and Barnes are arrested for Santiago’s murder. They’re assigned defense counsel from the JAG office, Lt. Daniel Kaffee (Tom Cruise), assisted by Lt. Sam Weinberg (Kevin Pollak) and Lt. Cmdr. JoAnne Galloway (Demi Moore). The defense faces a crucial ethical dilemma: accept a plea bargain for two men who blindly followed orders, or defend their innocence by implicating the officers who ordered the Code Red and orchestrated the cover-up. The JAG team must contend with prosecutor Captain Jack Ross (Kevin Bacon), who gathered overwhelming evidence to establish the accused’s guilt. The courtroom confrontation between Tom Cruise (Lt. Kaffee) and Jack Nicholson (Col. Jessup) is considered one of the greatest ever filmed. Kaffee abandons plea bargaining for moral principles when examining Jessup. Jessup believes Santiago’s death ensured Marines’ lives and justified any cover-up. The drama intensifies as Kaffee confronts Jessup, leading to the famous line, “You can’t handle the truth!” It is an iconic legal drama that excels in acting, storytelling, and legal accuracy. Its ethical dilemmas, especially in light of today’s Iran war and the Defense Secretary’s policies, remain relevant. The film skillfully combines a tense military thriller with character-driven conflict, exploring truth, morality, duty, and the consequences of blind loyalty. Director Rob Reiner doesn’t miss a beat, getting the most out of his material and actors. A Few Good Men will be screened at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, located at 801 Magnolia Ave., on Thursday, November 12. The doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone age 18 and above. The next movie will be Waking Ned Devine, a charming Irish comedy, scheduled for December 10 at 1 p.m.

articles.text: After two unforgettable decades of serving the Rockridge community, the beloved neighborhood institution Wood Tavern is closing its doors. To honor 20 years of incredible memories, fine dining, and community connection, the restaurant is hosting a spectacular farewell event: “A Pinot Paulée — Celebrating 20 Years of Wood Tavern” with all proceeds benefiting the East Bay Agency for Children (EBAC). All proceeds from the Pinot Paulée directly benefit EBAC’s mission to improve the well-being of children, youth and families by reducing the impact of trauma and social inequities. To learn more about East Bay Agency for Children, visit https://www.ebac.org. Rich Wood, of Wood Tavern (far right), raises a glass with the staff who bring the neighborhood favorite to life.

articles.text: Last Wednesday, October 28, was just three days before Halloween and time for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group’s annual pre-Halloween tour of the Mountain View Cemetery. Instead of meeting at the Exedra, the walkers assembled in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum. There was a big turnout of 56 walkers and five K-9 best friends on hand. The walkers were pleased to have Dawn Margolin, Cindy Wead, Beth Huges, Jean Hansen with K-9 best friends Halle and Hazel, and Pauline Marimos with them for the first time. Pauline is from France and working for a year in the area. She joins the walkers’ other young French lady participants, Juliane Jacqueline, Stacy Venetluhmamm, and Solene Francois. They add youth and more beauty to the group. This Wednesday walker tour was conducted for the sixth time by longtime Mt. View Cemetery docent Jane Leroe. She is a retired, groundbreaking San Francisco trial attorney who says she was a “feminist” before there were “feminists.” Jane has an extensive knowledge of the cemetery and loves to share it. After telling the group stories of “Famous Families” of the historic cemetery last year, Jane’s walk this morning was Part 2 of her family stories. Jane started off in front of the mausoleum with some general cemetery history. In the early 1860s a group of 12 leading local businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and the 13th mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, decided the area needed a better private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better for their final resting places. They bought 200 acres of cow-grazing fields at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery Association was established in 1863. It was officially dedicated on May 25, 1865, Memorial Day that year. It was thought that certainly the cemetery would always be far from the center of Oakland. Twenty-six acres were added later, so the cemetery has a total of 226 acres. About 175,000 people are buried at Mountain View, and there is room for an additional 175,000. Initially, those buried at Mt. View were all pretty much well-to-do, white Protestants. Catholics had created their own St. Mary’s Cemetery, just up the hill above Mt. View, in 1863 and that’s where they were buried. The founders’ contract with Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park and Stanford University, called for him to get $1,000, but it is uncertain if he ever got paid. Olmsted saw this as a Victorian garden cemetery. It was to be a private place, but not a park. Jane said he would not have approved of the ostentatious “Millionaires’ Row” on the hill above the cemetery’s main road. There were no women involved in the cemetery’s development. However, there were women behind these rich men, and some of them made good use of their deceased husbands’ money when they took up permanent residence at Mountain View. The stories of these and other women who were important in the early history of the area, and buried at Mt. View, are the focus of another tour that Jane leads and one the walkers look forward to. With this basic understanding of the cemetery’s history, Jane led the group up the main road and then a climb up a hill on the right. The walkers enjoyed the view of San Francisco on this mild, clear morning. Jane’s destination was the family plot of Ralph and Kate Kirkham. Ralph was a West Point graduate who served in the Mexican-American War in 1846 and was later assigned to the Presidio in San Francisco. After he left the army he became a businessman who sold supplies to the Union Army in the Civil War. He got rich and invested in real estate. Kate was an early feminist. In 1877, she founded the Fabiola Association and created the Fabiola Hospital in Oakland. It was named after Saint Fabiola, a fourth-century Roman Christian saint who renounced her wealth to build the first Christian public hospital for the poor and sick. Kate wanted her hospital to also provide free care for the area’s needy. She also founded a nursing school that was headed and staffed by only women. Sadly, their daughter, Leila Kirkham Yarde-Buller, went literally crazy after her husband and lover died and she had to be retrieved from Paris and later died in a mental facility. Down a rocky path were the graves of Edward and Eliza Head. Edward was blind, but that didn’t stop him from being elected to be a local judge. Eliza, his wife, read his cases to him. The Heads had money to send their daughter, Anna, to high school and UC Berkeley, and in 1887 she founded the Anna Head School near the UC Berkeley campus. In 1909 she sold the school to Mary E. Wilson, who renamed it the Anna Head School for Girls in 1919. In 1971 the school’s Board of Trustees established an all-boys school across the street called “The Royce School,” and in 1974 the two separate schools officially combined operations to become “The Head-Royce Schools.” In 1979 the transition was fully completed when the schools merged into a single, fully coeducational unit under its current name, The Head-Royce School. Harmon was an Oakland financier and mining magnate who made his fortune through Comstock Lode mines and in early Sacramento general stores. In 1878, he donated $15,000 (roughly $518,000 today) to build the university’s first indoor athletic facility and assembly hall, which was named “Harmon Gym,” with the gym only available to women students two days a week. He also built the historic Pardee Mansion in Oakland in 1868 and 1869, which is now the Pardee Home Museum. George followed his father into ophthalmology, and served on the Oakland City Council, as Mayor of Oakland from 1893 to 1895, and was the 21st Governor of California from 1903 to 1907. They did not use picks and shovels during California’s gold rush to make their fortunes but rather sold the miners the things they needed. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. The government stopped its appropriations in 1891, and the silk farm closed four years later. It was Piedmont’s only industry. articles.text: Happy November, all! GRATITUDE IN GOLD AND RED There is a moment each fall when the city seems to pause and show off. The trees along our streets have turned red and gold, and the light through them makes even a routine errand feel like a gift. It is a good time to count our blessings, and most of us have many. On the real estate front, the high end of the Piedmont market is drawing notice. Several architecturally stunning homes are currently listed, with more on the way, and they are likely to catch the eye of buyers who are benefiting from the wave of AI IPOs. How much that new wealth shapes the luxury market remains to be seen, and it will be interesting to watch. Beyond those listings, inventory remains limited as we wind down the year. For buyers, that means patience. For homeowners, it may mean opportunity. If you are considering selling in the near future, consider starting your preparations sooner rather than later. The Spring Market, usually the strongest of the year, often begins in late January, and the best-prepared homes tend to be ready when it does. Until then, let’s take a breath and enjoy the colors. MORTGAGE MONEY Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: It’s been a wild 60 days for mortgage rates. Rising oil prices, inflation concerns, and growing government debt pushed rates sharply higher in September (with the national average for a 30-year fixed mortgage approaching 7.75%). But in October, rates began moving back down and today sit closer to 7.25%. One reason for the improvement is the recent sell-off in tech stocks. Investors have become more cautious about the stock market and are moving money into safer investments like government bonds, helping bring mortgage rates back down. What continues to surprise me as a mortgage lender is just how much competition we’re still seeing for the best homes in the East Bay. Despite higher rates and all the economic uncertainty, I’m regularly seeing well-priced, beautifully presented homes attract multiple offers from motivated buyers. Meanwhile, homes that need work, are overpriced, or aren’t marketed properly can sit for weeks. The takeaway for homeowners is simple…buyers are still out there, but they’re being much more selective. I can’t remember a time when the difference between a well-prepared home and everything else has been so obvious.

The unpaid volunteer position of Piedmont school board member may have lost some of its glory when COVID closed the schools. Since then, the board has had to make tough calls like the 2024 Valentine’s Day announcement of staff cuts. Broad strokes of change, like the implementation of more AP and Honors classes, have also caused contentious debate, drawing parents, teachers and students to board meetings to make their complaints heard. Also adding to the lack of competition in the race was the departure of the previous superintendent in the middle of the nomination period for the school board. Were other candidates disheartened by the prospect of starting a school year without a leader?
